Attrition rate measures the percentage of employees who leave an organization over a set period. For most U.S. companies, that rate sits at 13% annually for voluntary departures, according to [Mercer's 2025 US Turnover Survey](https://www.imercer.com/articleinsights/workforce-turnover-trends) of 2,617 organizations. That's a meaningful improvement from 24.7% in 2022, but every percentage point still costs real money. [Gallup estimates](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/247391/fixable-problem-costs-businesses-trillion.aspx) that replacing a single employee costs 0.5x to 2x their annual salary - and voluntary departures cost U.S. businesses roughly $1 trillion per year collectively.

Whether you're an HR leader forecasting headcount, a recruiter filling the gaps attrition creates, or a people analytics team building retention dashboards, this guide covers everything you need. Start with the formula itself, then move through industry benchmarks by level, the real drivers of voluntary departures, and seven strategies that actually reduce unwanted attrition.

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - **Use the standard formula.** Attrition rate = (separations / average headcount) x 100, calculated across the full period rather than a multiplied monthly snapshot.
> - **Benchmark by industry.** U.S. voluntary attrition averages 13% ([Mercer 2025](https://www.imercer.com/articleinsights/workforce-turnover-trends)), but ranges from 8.2% in insurance to 26.7% in retail and wholesale.
> - **The cost is real.** Replacing one employee runs 0.5x to 2x annual salary, adding up to roughly $1 trillion per year across U.S. businesses ([Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/247391/fixable-problem-costs-businesses-trillion.aspx)).
> - **Career development is the top driver.** Lack of advancement beats pay as the #1 reason people quit, per McKinsey. Internal mobility and manager coaching move the needle the most.
> - **Better hiring cuts early attrition at the source.** Among the seven strategies, hiring for genuine fit is the most durable lever. Pin's AI matches candidates across 850M+ profiles and produces an 83% acceptance rate, meaning fewer role mismatches and fewer 90-day exits.

## What Is Attrition Rate?

Attrition rate is the percentage of employees who leave an organization during a specific time period and whose positions are not immediately backfilled. That last part matters. While "attrition" and "turnover" are often used interchangeably, [AIHR notes a technical distinction](https://www.aihr.com/blog/attrition-rate/): attrition refers to departures where the role is left open, while turnover implies the position gets filled with a new hire.

In practice, most HR teams and analysts use the terms synonymously. What matters more is understanding the types of attrition and tracking them separately:

-   **Voluntary attrition** - employees quit on their own (resignations, retirements). This is the number you most want to control.
-   **Involuntary attrition** - employer-initiated separations (terminations, layoffs, restructuring). SHRM's 2025 data shows a median involuntary rate of just 3%.
-   **Retirement attrition** - predictable but accelerating as Baby Boomers exit the workforce.
-   **Early attrition** - departures within the first 90 days, often signaling hiring or onboarding problems.

Not all attrition is bad. Losing low performers or employees in roles being automated can be healthy. The problem is _regrettable_ attrition - when your best people walk out the door and take institutional knowledge with them. While attrition measures all separations, [employee turnover rate](https://www.pin.com/blog/turnover-rate-guide/) focuses specifically on positions that need to be refilled - a distinction that changes how you budget for replacement hiring.

## How Do You Calculate Attrition Rate?

The standard formula used by SHRM, Mercer, and most HRIS platforms is straightforward, according to [AIHR](https://www.aihr.com/blog/attrition-rate/):

**Definition:** Attrition Rate (%) = (Number of Separations During Period / Average Number of Employees During Period) x 100

Where average headcount = (employees at start of period + employees at end of period) / 2.

### Monthly Calculation Example

Say your company started March with 500 employees and ended with 485. During March, 20 employees left (5 were laid off, 15 resigned).

-   Average headcount: (500 + 485) / 2 = 492.5
-   Total attrition rate: (20 / 492.5) x 100 = **4.06%**
-   Voluntary attrition rate: (15 / 492.5) x 100 = **3.05%**

### Annualizing the Rate

Don't just multiply a monthly rate by 12. That oversimplifies because it ignores compounding and seasonal variation. Instead, apply the formula across the full 12-month period using total annual separations and the average headcount for the year. If you must annualize a single month (say, for board reporting), use this adjustment:

**Annualized Rate = 1 - (1 - monthly rate)^12**

This accounts for the compounding effect and gives a more accurate projection than simple multiplication.

### What to Include (and Exclude)

Count all permanent employee separations: resignations, terminations, retirements, and deaths. Exclude temporary/contract workers, internal transfers (they didn't leave the organization), and employees on leave of absence. If you're tracking voluntary attrition specifically, exclude layoffs and terminations from the numerator.

## Attrition Rate Benchmarks by Industry (2025-2026)

The average attrition rate for U.S. workers is 13% for voluntary departures in 2024-2025, down from 17.3% the prior year, per [Mercer's 2025 survey](https://www.imercer.com/articleinsights/workforce-turnover-trends). But that average hides enormous variation across industries. Retail and wholesale leads at 26.7% - more than triple the 8.2% rate in insurance.

<figure style="margin:2rem 0;padding:0;line-height:0"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Voluntary Turnover Rate by Segment" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:12px"></figure>

Breaking down each segment reveals how different the hiring reality is from industry to industry. Retail sits at more than triple the rate of insurance, while the 13% all-industry average is pulled upward by that retail and wholesale outlier.

| Segment | Voluntary Turnover Rate | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retail & Wholesale | 26.7% | Mercer 2025 |
| Tech (Europe) | 17.4% | Ravio 2026 |
| All-Industries Average | 13.0% | Mercer 2025 |
| Engineering Function | 12.0% | Ravio 2026 |
| Insurance / Reinsurance | 8.2% | Mercer 2025 |
| Executives | 5.2% | Mercer 2025 |

[SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat) paints a similar picture from a different angle: the median voluntary turnover across 2,371 organizations was 9%, while the average hit 13%. The gap between median and average tells you something - a minority of organizations with very high churn pull the average up significantly.

### Benchmarks by Job Level

Mercer's data also breaks attrition down by organizational level, and the pattern is intuitive - the higher the role, the lower the turnover:

-   **Executives:** 5.2%
-   **Management:** 6.3%
-   **Sales professionals:** 7.3%
-   **Non-sales professionals:** 9.1%
-   **Para-professional / blue collar:** 12.5%

<figure style="margin:2rem 0;padding:0;line-height:0"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Voluntary Attrition Rate by Job Level" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:12px"></figure>

That gradient makes intuitive sense - executives have more equity, relationships, and status invested in their current role, which raises the psychological cost of leaving. Front-line workers face lower switching costs and often depart for marginal pay increases alone.

### What's a "Healthy" Attrition Rate?

There's no universal answer, but a few guidelines help. Rates below 10% are generally considered healthy for knowledge-work industries. For [retail and hospitality hiring](/blog/retail-hospitality-hiring/), 15-20% is more realistic. Extremely low attrition (below 3-4%) can actually signal stagnation - a lack of new perspectives entering the organization.

The goal isn't zero attrition. It's minimizing _regrettable_ attrition while maintaining a healthy flow of talent.

## How Much Does Employee Attrition Actually Cost?

Replacing an employee costs between 0.5x and 2x their annual salary, according to [Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/247391/fixable-problem-costs-businesses-trillion.aspx). [SHRM research (2024)](https://www.shrm.org/executive-network/insights/myth-replaceability-preparing-loss-key-employees) breaks down the range by seniority:

| Level | Replacement Cost (% of Annual Salary) | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry-Level | 30-50% | SHRM 2024 |
| Mid-Level | 125-150% | SHRM 2024 |
| Specialized / Senior | Up to 400% | SHRM 2024 |

These direct replacement costs serve as a useful baseline for calculating the real cost of attrition in your organization. The chart below visualizes the same data, making the cost escalation by seniority easier to see at a glance.

<figure style="margin:2rem 0;padding:0;line-height:0"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Replacement Cost by Seniority (% of Annual Salary)" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:12px"></figure>

And those are just the direct costs. [SHRM notes](https://www.shrm.org/executive-network/insights/myth-replaceability-preparing-loss-key-employees) that 60-70% of total attrition costs are hidden indirect expenses: lost productivity during the vacancy, reduced team morale, knowledge drain, customer relationship disruption, and the learning curve of new hires.

A concrete example: a 100-person company paying an average salary of $50,000 with 13% annual attrition would see 13 departures per year. At Gallup's conservative 0.5x-2x range, that's $325,000 to $1.3 million in annual replacement costs alone - before counting productivity losses.

This is why [tracking recruiting KPIs](https://www.pin.com/blog/recruiter-kpis-dashboard/) tied to retention matters as much as tracking time-to-fill or cost-per-hire. The cheapest hire in the world is expensive if they leave in six months.

## What Drives Employees to Leave?

The #1 driver of voluntary departures is lack of career development and advancement - not pay, not benefits, not workload. [McKinsey's research](https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/themes/why-employees-are-quitting-and-what-to-do-about-it) identifies four primary drivers, and they've remained remarkably consistent even as the post-pandemic labor market has cooled.

### The Top Drivers (Ranked)

1.  **Lack of career development** - McKinsey's #1 driver. LinkedIn's 2023 Workplace Learning Report found that 94% of employees said they'd stay longer at a company that invested in their career growth. Yet only 26% of workers report being highly satisfied with their promotion opportunities, per [Pew Research (December 2024)](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2024/12/10/job-satisfaction/).
2.  **Inadequate compensation** - The same Pew survey found only 30% of workers are highly satisfied with their pay. When people can get a 10-15% raise by switching jobs, loyalty has a price ceiling.
3.  **Poor leadership and management** - Uncaring or uninspiring leaders ranked third. The old adage holds: people don't leave companies, they leave managers.
4.  **Lack of meaningful work** - Employees who don't see purpose in what they do disengage, and disengagement is the first step toward the exit.

Here's the painful part: [Gallup found](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/247391/fixable-problem-costs-businesses-trillion.aspx) that 52% of voluntarily departing workers said their organization could have done something to prevent them from leaving. And 51% said no manager or leader had discussed their job satisfaction or future with the company in the three months before their departure.

Structurally, this isn't just an attrition problem. It's a management failure with a measurable cost.

### The Engagement Connection

U.S. employee engagement hit a 10-year low in 2024 - just 31% of workers reported being engaged, while 17% were actively disengaged, according to [Gallup (January 2025)](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/654911/employee-engagement-sinks-year-low.aspx). The areas with the sharpest declines were clarity of expectations (dropped from 56% to 46%), feeling cared about at work (47% to 39%), and development opportunities (36% to 30%).

Globally, [Gallup estimates](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/393497/world-trillion-workplace-problem.aspx) that disengaged employees cost the world economy $8.9 trillion in lost productivity - roughly 9% of global GDP. When engagement drops, attrition rises. They're two sides of the same coin.

## What Are the Most Effective Ways to Reduce Attrition?

Seven evidence-backed interventions can meaningfully cut voluntary departures: internal mobility extends tenure by 41% (LinkedIn), hybrid work reduces resignations by 33% (Stanford/PNAS, 2024), and high-quality recognition programs lower two-year turnover risk by 45% (Gallup-Workhuman, 2024). The research consistently points to structural changes that address the real reasons people leave - not perks.

### 1\. Invest in Career Development and Internal Mobility

Lack of growth is the #1 attrition driver (McKinsey), and the fix has clear ROI. [LinkedIn data](https://www.linkedin.com/business/talent/blog/talent-acquisition/how-internal-mobility-benefits-employers) shows that employees at companies with high internal hiring rates stay 41% longer on average - 7.4 years compared to 4.1 years at companies with low internal mobility.

What this looks like in practice: structured career pathing conversations (quarterly, not just during annual reviews), visible internal job boards, mentorship programs, and stretch assignments that let people build new skills without leaving the company.

### 2\. Fix Your Onboarding

Early attrition is a massive leak in most hiring pipelines. Research compiled by [AIHR](https://www.aihr.com/blog/employee-onboarding-statistics/) shows that 22% of workers have left a job within the first 90 days, and 60% of those early departures cite lack of training as the reason.

Conversely, Gallup found that managers who actively engage in onboarding produce new hires who are 3.4x more likely to describe their experience as exceptional. Onboarding isn't a one-day orientation - it's a 90-day (minimum) structured process that sets expectations, builds relationships, and ramps productivity.

### 3\. Offer Flexible Work Arrangements

A [Stanford study published in PNAS (June 2024)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38867040/) found that shifting from full-time office work to a hybrid schedule reduced resignations by 33%. That's not a marginal improvement - it's a third fewer people walking out the door.

Meanwhile, McKinsey found that 17% of workers who recently quit did so specifically because their employer changed office policies (typically return-to-office mandates). Flexibility isn't a perk anymore. It's a retention tool with measurable impact on attrition.

### 4\. Get Recognition Right

A [2024 Gallup-Workhuman longitudinal study](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/650174/employee-retention-depends-getting-recognition-right.aspx) of approximately 3,500 employees found that well-recognized workers are 45% less likely to turn over after two years. They're also 65% less likely to be actively job-seeking, and 9x more likely to be engaged.

The problem? Only 22% of employees report receiving the right amount of recognition - a number that hasn't budged since 2022. Recognition doesn't have to be expensive. It needs to be frequent, specific, and tied to the behaviors and outcomes the organization values.

### 5\. Pay Competitively (And Transparently)

With only 30% of workers highly satisfied with their pay ([Pew Research, December 2024](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2024/12/10/job-satisfaction/)), compensation remains a core attrition driver. But it's not always about paying the most - it's about paying fairly and transparently.

Conduct annual [compensation benchmarking](https://www.pin.com/blog/cost-per-hire-benchmarks/) against market rates. Share pay bands openly. Address compression issues proactively (when new hires earn more than tenured employees in the same role). Salary transparency laws in states like California, New York, and Colorado are accelerating this shift whether companies are ready or not.

### 6\. Improve Manager Quality

Poor leadership is McKinsey's #3 attrition driver, and it's the hardest to fix because it requires changing behavior, not just policy. But the data is clear: when Gallup tracked engagement declines from 2020 to 2024, the sharpest drops were in manager-dependent areas - feeling cared about at work (47% to 39%) and clarity of expectations (56% to 46%).

Train managers to hold regular one-on-ones, provide career development support, and have stay conversations (proactive retention check-ins) rather than only learning why someone left during an exit interview. Remember: 51% of departing employees said no leader discussed their satisfaction in the three months before they left.

### 7\. Hire Better From the Start

The best retention strategy starts before day one. When you hire candidates who genuinely fit the role, the team, and the trajectory of the company, they stick around longer. Poor job fit is an upstream cause of attrition that no amount of perks or retention programs can fix downstream.

## How Should You Track and Report Attrition?

Knowing your overall attrition rate is a start, but it's not enough for actionable decision-making. The most effective people analytics teams segment attrition data to identify patterns and target interventions where they'll have the most impact.

### Essential Segmentation Dimensions

-   **Voluntary vs. involuntary** - These require completely different responses. High voluntary attrition needs retention interventions. High involuntary attrition might signal hiring problems.
-   **Department / function** - Is engineering losing people at 2x the rate of marketing? That's a department-level issue, not a company-wide one.
-   **Tenure band** - High attrition in the 0-6 month band points to onboarding or hiring-fit issues. High [attrition at the 2-3 year mark](/blog/employee-tenure-funding-stage-study/) suggests career growth problems.
-   **Job level** - Mercer's data shows executive attrition at 5.2% versus 12.5% for front-line roles. These populations need different retention strategies.
-   **Regrettable vs. non-regrettable** - Losing a top performer is fundamentally different from losing a low performer. Track them separately.
-   **Manager** - If certain managers have consistently higher attrition, that's a coaching or accountability issue.

### Reporting Cadence

Track monthly, report quarterly, benchmark annually. Monthly tracking catches spikes early. Quarterly reporting gives leadership enough data to act without drowning in noise. Annual benchmarking against industry data (Mercer, SHRM, BLS) tells you how you compare to the market.

Build a simple [retention dashboard](https://www.pin.com/blog/recruiter-kpis-dashboard/) that shows: overall attrition rate (trailing 12 months), voluntary vs. involuntary split, attrition by department and tenure band, 90-day attrition rate (early turnover), and cost-of-attrition estimate. If any metric trends above your industry benchmark for two consecutive quarters, flag it for a root-cause analysis.

Supplement the dashboard with a monthly attrition report distributed to hiring managers. A one-page summary of the current monthly rate, trend direction, and any departments crossing benchmark thresholds is enough to trigger early intervention - before departures become a pattern.

## What Is the Current U.S. Quit Rate in 2026?

The broader labor market context matters for understanding your own attrition. **U.S. monthly quit rate: 1.9% (February 2026, [BLS JOLTS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/jolts.htm))**

That's well below the 3.0% peak during the Great Resignation in November 2021 and even below the 2024 annual average of 2.1%.

What does this mean? Workers are quitting at the lowest rate in years. The labor market has cooled. But don't confuse lower quit rates with higher satisfaction. [Gallup's engagement data](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/654911/employee-engagement-sinks-year-low.aspx) shows employees are less engaged than they've been in a decade. Many staff are staying in place not because they're satisfied, but because they perceive fewer opportunities elsewhere. When hiring picks up again, companies with unresolved retention problems could see a delayed attrition surge.

For the full 2024 picture: the [BLS annual averages](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/jolts_03112025.pdf) show a total separations rate of 3.3% monthly - composed of 2.1% quits, 1.1% layoffs and discharges, and 0.2% other separations.

## What Is the Difference Between Attrition, Turnover, and Retention?

These three terms get mixed up constantly, so here's a quick reference:

| Metric | What It Measures | Formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <strong>Attrition Rate</strong> | Employees who leave and aren't replaced | (Separations / Avg Headcount) x 100 |
| <strong>Turnover Rate</strong> | All employee departures (replaced or not) | (Departures / Avg Headcount) x 100 |
| <strong>Retention Rate</strong> | Employees who stayed over a period | ((Headcount End - New Hires) / Headcount Start) x 100 |

In practice, most organizations use "attrition" and "turnover" interchangeably. And that's fine for operational purposes. What matters is consistency - pick a definition, apply it the same way every period, and make sure everyone reading your reports understands what the number means.

Retention rate is simply the inverse perspective. If your annual attrition rate is 13%, your retention rate is roughly 87%. Some HR teams prefer to report retention because it frames the story positively, but the data underneath is identical.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a good attrition rate?

A good attrition rate depends on your industry. For knowledge-work sectors, below 10% annually is generally healthy. Retail and hospitality companies often see 20-25% as normal. Mercer's 2025 data shows the U.S. average voluntary rate at 13%, so anything consistently below your industry's average suggests effective retention practices.

### What does a zero attrition rate mean?

Zero attrition means no employees left during the period you measured. It sounds ideal, but a sustained 0% usually signals stagnation rather than health - no fresh perspectives are entering, and underperformers may be staying in roles they've outgrown. Most healthy knowledge-work teams run in the low single digits to low double digits, not zero.

### What does a 20% attrition rate mean?

At 20%, one in five employees left over the period, usually a year. In knowledge-work industries where sub-10% is the norm, that's high and worth investigating. High-turnover sectors like retail and hospitality, by contrast, treat 20-25% as closer to normal. Context matters more than the raw number - always compare against your industry benchmark.

### How do you calculate monthly attrition rate?

Divide the number of employees who left during the month by the average number of employees that month, then multiply by 100. For example, if 10 people left from an average headcount of 500, your monthly rate is 2.0%. To annualize, apply the full-year formula rather than simply multiplying by 12.

### What is the difference between attrition and turnover?

Technically, attrition refers to departures where the role isn't backfilled (headcount shrinks), while turnover includes all departures whether the role is filled or not. In practice, most HR teams and analytics platforms use the terms interchangeably. SHRM, Mercer, and BLS all report "turnover" data that encompasses both scenarios.

### Why is reducing attrition important for recruiters?

Every employee departure creates a requisition that recruiters must fill. At a replacement cost of 0.5x-2x annual salary (Gallup), high attrition drains recruiting budgets, extends time-to-fill, and forces teams into reactive hiring mode. Reducing unwanted attrition frees recruiters to focus on strategic [employer branding](https://www.pin.com/blog/employer-branding-guide/) and proactive talent pipeline building instead of backfill firefighting.

### Can AI help reduce employee attrition?

Yes, in two ways. First, AI-powered recruiting tools improve candidate-role fit from the start, reducing early attrition caused by mismatches. Pin is purpose-built for this use case: its 83% candidate acceptance rate and 14-day average fill time are direct results of AI matching that identifies both skills and role-context fit. Second, people analytics platforms use AI to identify attrition risk signals - disengagement patterns, compensation gaps, manager effectiveness - so HR can intervene before workers decide to leave.

### What is regrettable attrition?

Regrettable attrition is the departure of high-performing or high-potential employees an organization wanted to keep, as opposed to non-regrettable attrition, which is the exit of low performers or roles being automated away. Retention strategy hinges on this distinction, because losing top talent drains institutional knowledge and carries the steepest replacement cost. Most HR teams track regrettable and non-regrettable attrition separately, since a low overall rate can still hide a high regrettable rate. The goal is minimizing regrettable losses while keeping a healthy flow of talent.

### What does a zero attrition rate mean?

A zero attrition rate means no employees left during the measured period. Though it sounds ideal, sustained 0% attrition is usually a warning sign rather than a goal. Such stability can mask a stagnant workforce, limited internal mobility, or employees staying only because they lack better options. Healthy organizations expect some natural attrition. The real target is minimizing regrettable attrition, the loss of people you wanted to keep, not driving total attrition to zero.

## Key Takeaways

-   The standard attrition rate formula is (separations / average headcount) x 100. Track voluntary and involuntary separately.
-   U.S. voluntary attrition averages 13% (Mercer 2025), ranging from 8.2% in insurance to 26.7% in retail.
-   Replacement costs range from 30-50% of salary for entry-level roles up to 400% for specialized positions.
-   The #1 driver of voluntary attrition is lack of career development - not compensation.
-   52% of departing employees say their organization could have prevented them from leaving.
-   Proven interventions include internal mobility (+41% longer tenure), hybrid work (-33% resignations), and recognition programs (-45% turnover risk).
